provenance.provider: NYC GeoSearch (Pelias over the NYC Property Address Directory)
provenance.note: Byte-identical to the live response. Nothing edited, redacted, or synthesised.

why_this_query.text: 'New York, NY' is the single most common location string in the corpus and the exact input city.md §4.3 forbids sending to a geocoder. That prohibition was written from reasoning rather than measurement. This fixture is the measurement, and it is worse than the reasoning predicted.

what_it_establishes.the_design_doc_was_too_generous: city.md claimed Pelias would answer with the city centroid at a good score. It does not. It returns NEW YORK HOSPITAL — a specific building at First Avenue and 68th Street — at confidence=1, match_type=exact, accuracy=point. A centroid at least sits in the middle of the city and looks like an approximation. This looks like an answer.
what_it_establishes.the_provider_reports_maximum_confidence_: confidence=1 and match_type=exact, both higher than the correct result for a real address (0.8, fallback). Pelias is not wrong on its own terms — it matched the words 'New York' against venue names, exactly. It is answering a different question from the one the caller meant.
three_independent_signals_expose_it: geocoding.query.parsed_text has no `housenumber` key at all — Pelias itself reports that it did not see an address.
Every returned feature has housenumber=null and a `street` that is really a venue name ('NEW YORK HOSPITAL').
addendum.pad.bin is '1000000' on two of three results — the Manhattan placeholder BIN, meaning the PAD has no building for this record. A real address returns a real BIN ('1087186').
what_it_establishes.why_the_gate_is_still_the_right_defence: Any of the three signals above could be checked after the fact, and the adapter checks them. But the cheapest and most robust protection remains never sending the query: a request not made cannot be misinterpreted, cannot cost a rate-limit slot, and cannot be defeated by a provider changing how it scores.
